'''John Charles Chenoweth McKinsey''' (30 April 1908 – 26 October 1953), usually cited as '''J. C. C. McKinsey''', was an American mathematician known for his work on [[game theory]] and [[mathematical logic]],<ref name=histsoc>[http://histsoc.stanford.edu/pdfmem/McKinseyJ.pdf Memorial Resolution] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727062509/http://histsoc.stanford.edu/pdfmem/McKinseyJ.pdf |date=2011-07-27 }}, Stanford Historical Society</ref> particularly, [[modal logic]].<ref>"One of the very first applications of [[topology]] to (modal) logic is McKinsey’s 1941 paper." [http://www.canbaskent.net/logic/early/top.pdf Top of-the Logic] - Can Baskent</ref>

==Biography==
McKinsey received B.S. and M.S. degrees from [[New York University]] and a Ph.D. degree in 1936 from the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=31457|name=John Charles Chenoweth McKinsey}}</ref> He was a Blumenthal Research Fellow at New York University from 1936 to 1937 and a [[Guggenheim Fellow]] from 1942 to 1943.<ref name=histsoc/><ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130415000835/http://www.gf.org/fellows/9746-john-charles-mckinsey|title=J(ohn) C(harles) McKinsey - John Simon Guggeheim Memorial Foundation}}</ref>  He also taught at [[Montana State College]], and in Nevada, then Oklahoma, and in 1947 he went "to a research group at [[Douglas Aircraft Corporation]]" that later became the [[RAND Corporation]].<ref name=feferman/>{{rp|p. 161}}

McKinsey worked at RAND until he was fired in 1951. The FBI considered him a [[security risk]] because he was a [[homosexual]], in spite of the fact that he was an open homosexual who had been in a [[committed relationship]] for years. He complained to his superior "How can anyone threaten me with disclosure when everybody already knows?"<ref name=RAND>{{cite book | last = Abella | first = Alex | title = Soldiers of reason : the Rand Corporation and the rise of the American empire | publisher = Mariner Books | location = Boston | year = 2009 | isbn = 978-0-15-603344-2 |page=74}}</ref>

From 1951 he taught at [[Stanford University]], where he was later appointed a Full Professor in the Department of Philosophy,<ref name=histsoc/> where he worked with [[Patrick Suppes]] on the axiomatic foundations of [[classical mechanics]].<ref name=feferman/>{{rp|p. 232}}  He committed suicide<ref name=RAND/> at his home in [[Palo Alto]] in 1953.<ref name=histsoc/>
